name: Magnification
rule: Magnification = image size ÷ real size. Put both sizes in the same unit before you divide. Magnification has no units.
trick: Cover the one you want: real size = image size ÷ magnification. 1 mm = 1000 µm, so change mm to µm by multiplying by 1000.

another.text: A photo of your face on a big poster looks much bigger than your real face. Magnification just says how many times bigger the picture is than the real thing.
another.example:
Real face: 20 cm
Poster face: 100 cm
100 ÷ 20 = ×5

steps.say: Magnification = image size ÷ real size. The sizes must be in the same unit first.

steps.ask: The units are different. What is 9 mm in µm?
steps.then: 1 mm is 1000 µm, so 9 mm is 9 × 1000 = 9,000 µm.
steps.hint: Micrometres are smaller, so there are more of them: multiply by 1000.

steps.then: Image size on top, real size underneath.
steps.hint: Image ÷ real. The image is the bigger number.

questions.stem: An image is 18 mm long and the real object is 0.2 mm long. What is the magnification?
An image is 10 mm across at ×250. What is the real size?

name: Variables
rule: The independent variable is the one you change. The dependent variable is the one you measure. Control variables are everything else you keep the same so the test is fair.
trick: Ask three questions: what did they change, what did they measure, what did they keep the same?

examples.text: Change the length of a wire, measure its resistance
examples.note: Independent: length. Dependent: resistance. Control: thickness and material of the wire.

another.text: Imagine racing toy cars down a ramp to see which ramp height is fastest. You change the height. You time the car. You use the same car every time, or the race is not fair.
another.example:
Changed: ramp height
Measured: time
Kept the same: the car

walkthrough.board: A student grows cress seedlings with a lamp at different distances and measures the height of each seedling after 7 days.

steps.say: Every investigation has a variable you change, one you measure, and the ones you keep the same.

steps.ask: What did the student change on purpose?
steps.hint: Which one did they choose before starting?

steps.then: Every seedling grows for 7 days, so the time is kept the same.
steps.hint: Look for something the same for every seedling.

questions.stem: A student times how long seeds take to germinate at different temperatures. What is the dependent variable?
questions.why: The time is what is measured, so it is the dependent variable.

questions.stem: A student tests how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed. Which is a control variable?
questions.why: Temperature also affects the rate, so it must be kept the same. The lamp distance is the independent variable.

name: Relative formula mass
rule: The relative formula mass (Mr) is the sum of the relative atomic masses (Ar) of every atom in the formula.
trick: A small number after a symbol counts that atom only. A number after a bracket multiplies everything inside the bracket.

another.text: Think of a fruit bowl. An apple weighs 10 and a banana weighs 20. A bowl with 2 apples and 1 banana weighs 10 + 10 + 20 = 40. Mr is the same: add up the weight of every atom.

steps.say: Count every atom in the formula, then add up their relative atomic masses.

steps.ask: How many hydrogen atoms are there?
steps.then: The small 2 after H means two hydrogens: 2 × 1 = 2.
steps.hint: Look at the small number after H.

steps.ask: Sulfur has no small number. How much does it add?

steps.then: The Mr of sulfuric acid is 98.

questions.stem: What is the Mr of NaCl? (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)
What is the Mr of CH₄? (C = 12, H = 1)

name: Balancing equations
rule: Atoms are not made or destroyed, so a balanced equation has the same number of each type of atom on both sides. Balance by putting big numbers in front of formulas.
trick: Never change the small numbers inside a formula; that changes the substance. Only add big numbers in front, and balance one element at a time.

examples.note: 4 H and 2 O on each side.
Changing H₂O to H₂O₂ makes a different substance.

another.text: Building with blocks: if you start with 4 red blocks and 2 blue ones, the model you build must use exactly 4 red and 2 blue. Nothing appears and nothing vanishes.
another.example:
Start: 4 red, 2 blue
End: 4 red, 2 blue

steps.say: Count each type of atom on both sides. Fix one element at a time with a big number in front.

steps.ask: How many Cl atoms are on the right?
steps.then: MgCl₂ has two chlorines, but HCl on the left has only one.

steps.ask: What goes in front of HCl?
steps.hint: You need 2 chlorines on the left.

steps.ask: Now count hydrogen: 2HCl has 2 H, and H₂ has 2 H. Is it balanced?
steps.then: Mg, Cl and H all match, so the equation is balanced.

questions.why: 2NaCl has 2 Na, so 2Na is needed on the left.
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O has 1 C, 4 H and 4 O on each side.

name: Using a physics equation
sub: Put the numbers in, then work it out
rule: Write the equation, put each number in place of its word, then calculate. Check the units are the ones the equation expects, such as kg, m and s.
trick: Do any squaring first. In kinetic energy = 0.5 × m × v², square the speed before you multiply.

examples.text: V = I × R, I = 2 A, R = 6 Ω
KE = 0.5 × m × v², m = 4 kg, v = 3 m/s

another.text: An equation is like a recipe card with gaps. The question tells you what goes in each gap. Fill them in, then follow the recipe.
another.example:
power = energy ÷ time
energy 600 J, time 20 s
600 ÷ 20 = 30 W

walkthrough.board: KE = 0.5 × m × v², m = 6 kg, v = 4 m/s

steps.say: Put each number in place of its letter, then work it out in the right order.

steps.ask: Which do you work out first?

questions.stem: Power = potential difference × current. What is the power when V = 12 V and I = 3 A?
Density = mass ÷ volume. A 40 g object has a volume of 8 cm³. What is its density?

name: Units and prefixes
rule: Physics equations use standard units: J, W, A, m, kg and s. Convert first. Kilo (k) means × 1000 and milli (m) means ÷ 1000.
trick: kW to W: × 1000. mA to A: ÷ 1000. g to kg: ÷ 1000. Minutes to seconds: × 60.

another.text: A kilo is a big bag holding 1000 little ones. A milli is one tiny crumb, a thousandth of the whole. Going from bags to little ones, you get more, so multiply.

walkthrough.board: A 1.5 kW heater runs for 2 minutes. Energy = power × time

steps.say: Convert to watts and seconds before using the equation.

name: Rearranging an equation
sub: Get the one you want on its own
rule: If the quantity you want is multiplied by something, divide by it on both sides. For A = B × C: B = A ÷ C and C = A ÷ B.
trick: Check by putting your answer back in: B × C should give A again. If it does not, you divided the wrong way round.

another.text: If 3 bags hold 12 sweets in total, each bag holds 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Total = number of bags × sweets in each, so to find one of the two you divide the total by the other.

walkthrough.board: F = m × a. F = 600 N, a = 2 m/s². Find m.

steps.say: m is multiplied by a. To get m on its own, divide both sides by a.

steps.hint: Undo × a by dividing by a.

steps.then: 600 N, the force in the question, so 300 kg is right.

questions.stem: distance = speed × time. A car goes 150 m at 10 m/s. How long does it take?
V = I × R. Which gives R?
questions.why: Divide both sides by I: R = V ÷ I.
